title: Trust Region Q Adjoint Matching
claim: Naive critic-guided fine-tuning drifts destructively from the pretrained policy; ours bounds deviation with an adaptive trust region and wins on benchmarks.
layout: 2 panels: 3-step left-to-right cartoon with arrows, plus bar chart on right
description: The figure has two panels. Panel (a) on the left shows three rounded boxes joined by black arrows. The first, in gray, shows a single smooth S-shaped gray trajectory labeled 'useful pretrained policy'. The second, also gray, shows the same trajectory with red branches that diverge from it. It is labeled 'destructive drift, e.g., QAM, QAM-E'. The third box is orange-tinted and shows the gray trajectory enclosed by two orange curves with arrowheads. It is labeled 'controlled deviation' and 'adapts via dual descent', with a λ symbol. Panel (b) on the right is a horizontal bar chart of offline RL success rate on OGBench. caption: TRQAM builds adaptive trust-region control into the SOC sampling process. (a): Each curve is a sampling trajectory of the flow policy, from noise $X_0$ to action $X_1$. Fixed-temperature methods such as QAM and QAM-E [ref] suffer from destructive drift, where small critic errors can be exponentially amplified into large policy errors ([ref]). TRQAM instead bounds the deviation from the pretrained policy through a trust-region parameter $\lambda$ internalized in the SOC sampling process, which limits how far critic errors can move the policy. (b): Offline RL success rate on 50 OGBench [ref] tasks, where TRQAM outperforms all baselines.
abstract: Off-policy reinforcement learning of pretrained flow policies remains challenging due to the instability of optimization arising from the multi-step sampling process. Recently, Q-learning with Adjoint Matching (QAM) addressed this by recasting policy improvement as a stochastic optimal control (SOC) problem guided by a learned critic. However, QAM inherits a fundamental fragility of critic-guided improvement, since small critic errors can be exponentially amplified and often lead to performance collapse. This paper introduces Trust Region Q Adjoint Matching (TRQAM), a stable off-policy fine-tuning algorithm that adaptively controls the path-space KL between the fine-tuned and pretrained policies through projected dual descent. Specifically, we adapt a trust-region parameter $Î»$ inside the sampling process of the flow policy and prove that $Î»$ exactly weights the path-space KL in the SOC objective. As a result, our method can tightly control the deviation from the pretrained policy within a prescribed KL budget, achieving stable off-policy RL. Through experiments on 50 OGBench tasks, TRQAM consistently outperforms prior methods in both offline RL and offline-to-online RL. In particular, TRQAM achieves an overall success rate of 68% in offline RL, substantially improving over the strongest baseline at 46%.
